title: Bali keeps his word
hookLine: warned it's a trap, a king keeps his word anyway
carry: satya: a word given is a word kept
tomorrow: the water touches the ground. how big does the small boy get?

lines: THE WATER IS IN HIS HAND.
cards: Somebody always says it right before a signature: wait, don't sign that. Bali's teacher, Shukra, leans close at the sacrifice. That boy is Vishnu, he says.
Those three steps will take everything you have. Take the promise back. The water for the gift is already in Bali's hand.
And Bali doesn't take it back.

teach.b: Shukra makes a good case. A promise that would ruin you, he says, can be set aside, and no one would blame you.

teach.h: THE EARTH CAN'T CARRY A LIAR.
teach.b: Bali answers with a line the Purana keeps: the earth can carry any weight except a person who lies. He's Prahlada's grandson, and if this really is Vishnu asking, what is there to lose? Shukra curses him for it.
Bali pours the water anyway, and the gift is made. That water matters.

In Hindu rites a gift or a vow is sealed with water, and you can still see it: at the start of a puja, many Hindus hold a little water in the right palm, say what they're offering and why, and let it go.
It's called sankalpa, the resolve. Once it's poured, it's given.
Bali is honored for that: satya, truth to your word. Now the week in one breath. The Lord lives in every being, said a child in a demon's palace.
He stepped out of a stone pillar to keep his devotee's word. Bhakti at its height asks for nothing, and every asker is still welcome. The fierce god's hand on a child's head is a blessing.
A vow offers what you can't fix. Santosha: enough is a practice. And Prahlada's grandson pours the water.

how: Many Hindus begin a puja with a sankalpa, holding water in the palm while stating the offering, then releasing it. The Bhagavata Purana tells Vamana's story at length, and in Kerala the festival of Onam is kept in memory of King Bali, known there as Mahabali.

o: the teacher who warned Bali to take it back
the water poured out to seal a gift
Vishnu's small form, who asked Bali for three steps

games.q: the week, in pairs — tap them.
p: every lock held; help came between

s: Bali never knew who the boy really was
Shukra told him: that boy is Vishnu. he gave anyway.
Bali is Prahlada's grandson in the Bhagavata
the man-lion's boy and the generous king are one family.
Narasimha broke the wording of the boon
he kept every word: the doorway, the dusk, the lap, no weapon.

games.q: at a puja, the priest has you hold water in your palm, say what you're offering, then pour it out. a friend asks why. by Bali's story?
o: it's sankalpa: the water seals your word, like Bali's gift.
it's to wash your hands before the prasad.
it's for luck; what you say doesn't really matter.
games.why: Bali held the water, heard Shukra's warning, and poured it anyway. once the water's poured, the word is given.

practice: If you pray, hold a little water in your right palm, or just cup the hand, and say one promise you mean to keep, small or large. Then let the water go, or open the hand, the way Bali poured. Breathe with it for the sit.
If it feels heavy, let each breath out carry a little of the weight.

wordCard.voice: Vamana: the small form of Vishnu, and the king who was warned who he was, and gave anyway.

orig.note: Sanskrit: truth, being true to your word. Bali's answer to Shukra turns on it.

carryVoice: The line: satya, a word given is a word kept. Bali poured the water anyway. That's the week.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.19–8.20 (Shukra's warning; Bali's answer; the curse; the gift)
Bhagavata Purana 7.5–7.10 and 8.15–8.19 (the week's look-back: Prahlada, the boon, the boons refused, the hand, Aditi, the three steps)
